utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber has verified the quotes you gave as far as Mr. Celic is concerned. They're not fully accurate. Your quote went beyond what was really said. Would you be very precise in putting to a witness what other witnesses have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say that I did not put what Celic said in court, or it was just -- I was referring only to this witness's statement at the time when the counsel objected that I was dealing with the matter which I had not explored with a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll tell you at a later moment this morning where the problem lies. Meanwhile, Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, your examination will now continue. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By the 27th of August, were you aware that there had been a report from UNCRO officers on the 25th of August at -- in the evening to the Knin garrison that there had been a fire in Grubori at that time? And by "fire," I mean arson rather than any other form of activity.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember from certain conversations we had, I think that there was the information that the UNCRO officials reported some events in the area, but I didn't know exactly what kind of event was involved at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that on the 27th of August, that the UN CIVPOL had reported to the Knin police that there had been some form of hostile activity in Grubori on the 25th of August, that the UN CIVPOL had reported to Knin police on the 25th of August that there had been something that had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: My answer to the question would be that I don't know the precise date when I received that information. I can't remember who I received it from either. I know that subsequently the information got about that the UN CIVPOL had been informed of the events in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, were you aware on the 27th of August that the Knin police had been to the Plavno valley, as a result of the report from UN CIVPOL of something happening in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I believe that there was information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 27th of August, were you aware that a Lieutenant Dondo from the Knin garrison had visited Grubori on the 26th of August and made a report to the Knin local police that some people had been killed in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As I've already said, there was information to the effect that the civilian police had been informed by the international forces of that having happened in the area, but I'm not familiar with the name of Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To be more specific, Dondo was, at that time, working in the Knin garrison, and he had been to the Knin police on the 26th of August and filed a report there of what happened. Did you know that, that someone from the Knin garrison had done that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. The only information I had was that the police was informed of there having been this event in the area. The civilian police, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, might I seek clarification from the witness. You said, "the only information I had." Could you specify the date and time when you had this information available. Was it when you were still in Zagreb? Was it when you were travelling? Was it upon your arrival in Gracac? Was it -- could you please detail the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, I received the information when I was in the area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only -- that is, after you had visited ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I meant was that the information was received probably at the time of the visit to Grubori. That's why I said in the general area of Knin, at the time of the visit to the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 27th of August, who did you think was investigating what had happened in Grubori on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was not informed of the fact that an actual investigation took place. If it did, then it must have taken place on the 26th, for that there was none on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on the 27th of August, were you aware of an official report dated the day before, on the 26th, from the special police as to what had happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. I did not have an opportunity to see the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to ask you if you saw any of the special police documents before the 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Since I wasn't in the action and I wasn't part of the command of the action, I didn't have occasion to see the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I ask in cross-examination. Your Honour, this there is a matter I need to bring to the Court's attention, and it concerns Prosecution Exhibits P1151, Exhibit P1152. These are the transcripts of this witness's video interview. When my learned friend for the Prosecution was asking questions on Friday, and I saw the transcript of the -- of the questions and a passage that she read out, I went to Exhibit P1152. In my version of this document, this is at page 46. There's another version of the document. It's the same translation but a bigger type, I think, where it's page 49. I can give the Court those references. And it concerns something mentioned as being reported speech by Mr. Casey - and I know Your Honours has already referred to this questioning of Mr. Casey - and the issue of the party line. I looked at the Croatian interpreter's interpretation of that question, and I didn't see a word that I know one of the two, probably, of Lijna which I know means line. And I saw a word called smislu, and I noticed that in Mr. Turkalj's response, he used that word, smislu, and I noticed the interpreter's translation of the word sense. So I had that looked at by our translator and interpreter who works for us, and it was confirmed to me that this passage of Mr. Casey's speech was not accurately translated to the witness. The witness gave his response and what we have in our record here, which is not a matter for the witness, but it's a matter of the state of the exhibit, was that the translations by the interpreter were wrong. The word smislu means sense, and it does not mean line, party line. I then caused, over the weekend, not to have the whole document reviewed, as we didn't have the time, but just passages that I was particularly interested in, and I noticed on several occasions that this had occurred during this video interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say that the witness may be asked to take off the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness has a certain interest himself in it as well, Ms. Mahindaratne, because -- we're talking about apparent errors in translation made during the interview which is a matter -- of course, Mr. Kay, I do not expect to you go through every detail of the same. But here we have one word which is given as an example by Mr. Kay, and he says there is are more. I do not expect him, and I would agree with you that it would be inappropriate to go through all the details of how a question was mistranslated or whether an answer was mistranslated. We will have to sort that out ourselves and not in the presence of the witness. But Mr. Kay is drawing your attention to mistakes in translation, at least possible mistakes in the translation during the interview. If I say translation, I should say interpretation. That is a matter for all of us to be aware of, if there is merit in what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the case, Mr. President. We would have to verify, and I'm not in any way challenging if Mr. Kay has already checked on this, but we would have to verify what is exactly the problem with the translation and to discuss this in the presence of the witness may open unnecessary opportunities, Mr. President, particularly the examination is not concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. The advantage is that we become aware of possible sources of confusion, and it should not, to that extent, I agree, but I think I have been clear enough to Mr. Kay in this respect, that if the matter will be raised during further examination, then, of course, we have the Croatian text there, so that we can verify on the spot whether there's any translation or interpretation issue, and I would not expect anyone to abuse the situation, and if anyone tries, then the first thing, of course, the Chamber will do is to put an end to any abuse, because we have a possibility to verify immediately what the issue is. And tomorrow perhaps Mr. Turkalj is not there anymore. Mr. Kay, you have pointed at possible errors in interpretation during these interviews. May I take it that you want this to be verified in full detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was the one that brought my attention to it, and caused me to look at certain other passages, and if I tell the Court what the problem seems to me to have been, and it's understandable, a long question is asked, the interpreter doesn't translate every word, I'm not pointing out passages where a word was missed. I'm simply not interested in that, but there are very significant passages of, in my view, interest to the resolution of this matter and indeed would be of interest to all the parties, and I had it checked over the weekend just to satisfy myself, and I have been briefed on the matter. In a sense, I was alerting Your Honours to this, and then proposing a way of dealing with it. I was going to put these passages into a schedule with what we say is the problem with the passage, serve that on the Prosecution, and then they can take instructions on the matter, and then we can see if there is any disagreement. I'm confident in the level of advice I have been given on this. And then to alert the Trial Chamber so that there can be some sort of filing rather like we've done with the stipulation so that the Trial Chamber is not working on what, to my mind, is patently wrong information, which I think would be highly embarrassing for everyone if anyone looked at the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- acceptable to you. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Kay, but I noticed the same thing on several occasions with respect to some of the translations in the transcript, and I would point the Court specifically to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, we try to avoid to point at certain portions of the interview in order not, because otherwise, we would really have to ask the witness to take his earphones off. If there matters which are urgent and for which the Chamber could not wait until we have gone through an exercise as suggested by Mr. Kay, then we should ask the witness to take earphones off if it would influence the examination still to be expected today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Sorry, Your Honour. I didn't see he still had his headphones on. I do think that in this instance, and I won't obviously talk about the specific portions of the interview of the transcript, that there are significant issues with respect to the translation in certain areas that are obviously very important to the case. So I will leave it at that. And what I'll do is similar to what Mr. Kay has suggested. I'll put together those areas which I think have been either not completely translated or mistranslated and submit them in a schedule. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if there are matters which directly have an impact on the testimony of the witness given these days, and, Mr. Kay, you gave one example. And it was put to the witness -- I don't know whether the wording exactly then was had a great impact on his answers, but if there's any matter which has a direct impact, of course, the witness is still here, so I would then invite you, Mr. Kuzmanovic, or you, Mr. Kay, to put questions to the witness in relation to those portions, not necessarily pointing at what was mistranslated, et cetera, but just to verify through question and answer what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Normally I would agree with that procedure, but in this instance, I think the answer itself that the witness gave is fine to the question. It's what has been translated is what isn't fine. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is no need. It has no impact, then it would -- the matters could be repaired in the way Mr. Kay has suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I considered the amendments or the statements the witness made when he came in and looked at that and, so to speak, pieced matters together in my own mind which caused this to become from an academic exercise to a more practical assessment of how we deal with it. May I say, we're not grooming this transcript into a perfect every word, because I have no interest in that, and simply, the resources would not justify it. But it was the passages that I believe are of significance to my case, and the exercise I propose would be confined to that, rather than the whole 500 pages because it would simply be a task where I would have no interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it puts the Chamber on notice that there may be other areas as well which calls for great caution in using this statement, and the Chamber will certainly keep that not only in the back of its mind but even in front of its mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. And like with Mr. Theunens, we'll endeavour to get on with this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I just want to clarify a couple of issues in looking at both one of your statements P1150 in conjunction with your transcript. And the first issue I'd like to address with you is your description of the attack by the special police on the morning of the 4th of August. If at any point you need additional clarification, please stop me, and I will attempt to so. On page -- on P1150 of your transcript and this is at page 78, line 21, you noted that the plan of the attack was in five or six -- five to six directions. And then moving ahead two pages to page 80 on that same exhibit: "And each direction that was determined had a support of one artillery group that was supposed to escort them to follow them." Now, in your transcript at page 13700, you were asked some additional questions. And I'd just like to go through this and just clarify this. You were asked some additional questions by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, and this is on page 13700, beginning on line 23, talking about -- line 22. "Can you describe for us in what way the artillery of the special police was used? Who called for that support and who provided clearance for the use of artillery? What was the procedure like?" "Answer: The procedure was very simple. Every axis of attack including the main and auxiliary ones had a rocket artillery battery designed for their purpose. Every commander of every axis referred to their own battery that they had assigned to them as their support and asked for the type of support they needed." So clarifying this, Mr. Turkalj, in each particular direction that the special police was going, was an artillery battery attached to that direction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on page 13697 of your transcript you were asked: "Can you tell us what sort of artillery of their own did the special police have that they could use in Operation Storm?" Your answer was: "As regards to their own artillery, they had mixed artillery batteries comprising of 120-millimetre mortars and 128-millimetre RAK-12 rocket launchers." Now I want to clarify one issue on that score, and that has to with -- it could have just been something that was a mistake in the transcript, I'm not sure, but nevertheless, in your testimony of last week, and this is on page 13693, at line 6 you said: "Every commander along his axis of attack had a multi-barreled rocket launcher 120-millimetre of the RAK type." When you said 120-millimetre multi-barrel rocket launcher, did you intend to say a 128-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: If it was a multi-barrel rocket launcher, then the calibre was 128.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Mahindaratne asked you a series of questions about -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before you continue, I had some difficulties in finding your reference on page 78, and that is 78 out of 138, I think you said line 21. I couldn't find that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. It should have been page 78, line 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 28 is an empty the line for me but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the -- I'm looking at 1150, and I don't know if it was -- came up differently in the e-court, but this is what I have printed out. At the bottom it says page 78 of 137, which I believe is 1150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have got 138, so there is -- apparently you're working from a copy which is not exactly the same as the one uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, the -- I found the same page, and I'm going along page 78 of 137, Mr. President, If I could just have a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the whole of the document is 137 instead of 138, then it sounds logical to look at 77 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what I'm doing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was told I have been informed that on e-court, it has come up as 138 because the last page is a blank page, but that page had been, for some reason, counted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have two kind of page numbering, Ms. Mahindaratne. The one is the e-court page numbering, the electronic numbering, but there is also the print at the bottom of the page, which in e-court also says 77 of 138. Let me check the last page. The last page is an empty page, that is true, but I do not find anything on 77 either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that the attention has already been drawn to this -- what I now find, and it's kept away from -- from me, perhaps for very good reasons, in order not to be bothered by it. I do understand that the hard copy that the parties are working off is a different version than the one uploaded in e-court, and that there has been a invitation to upload there e-court the version, which is the version used by the witness, because otherwise we get a huge puzzle at any later point in time. I leave it for the time being, not being aware that it was touching upon a far larger problem than just not being able to find the reference, Mr. Kehoe. Let's proceed for the time being. I take it that you quoted with the precision I'm used to, as far as you are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you were referred to P1154 during your examination with the Prosecution. Now, this document in the -- the first two -- the listing of expenditures of rounds and the request by General Markac of a resupply, the first is mines that's 122-millimetre, that would from the mortars. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, did you mean 120-millimetre as the document reads? [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The mines for the 122-millimetres, those are 120-millimetre rounds for the mortars that the units had, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The document reads mines, 122-millimetres, but these are actually rounds for mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They are actually rounds for mortars. That is what I was getting at. And the --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the number 2 is missiles, 128-millimetre. Those are likewise rounds for the 128-millimetre RAK multi-barrel rocket launcher that you were using, right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: These are rockets for the RAK-12 type 128-millimetre piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, these two entries, number 1 and 20 -- and number 2, they were for weapons that the individual special police units had and began to use as the attack began on the 4th, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you told us on page 13706 that depending on the phase of the action the most -- the most artillery was spent breaking through the first line of defence. So would it be fair to say, based on your testimony and this, the majority of these rounds were expended on the 4th, when you were trying to get through the ARSK defences?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there is nothing in this list for the expenditure of rounds for a 122-millimetre Grad rocket system, is there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, it wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, according to P619, which is the report that was filed with General Cervenko on the 26th of November, 2001, the 122 multi-barrel rocket launcher was the one that was at -- provided to the special police at the HV level, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we have that document that Mr. Kehoe is referring to on the screen, so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure. P619. It is in the B/C/S, it's page 23; and in the English, it's page 19. This was a document that was referred -- referred to by Ms. Mahindaratne during the course of direct. I'm told that the particular insertion that we're talking about, Mr. President, is in the English on page 19 and in the B/C/S page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar informs me that he has a two-page document on P619. I haven't found --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I think I misspoke. It's P614. I apologise. I think I misspoke in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, you will get another document soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's the document we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, I do believe that we talked about this during the course of your direct examination and certainly during the cross by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. And you see about midway through the page, certainly on the English, and I see it's towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, that the special police was strengthened by HV rocket and artillery forces with the strength of reinforced 130-millimetre cannon platoon, reinforced 122-millimetre D30 Howitzer platoon and the one 122 Grad rocket system. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just being clear, the 128-millimetre multi-barrel rocket launchers were deployed by the special police throughout the axes of attack, and the 122-millimetre rocket system was at the HV level. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The multiple rocket launcher of 122-millimetre calibre was attached by the HV for the purposes of that operation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just cover a couple of smaller instances, and one I would like to talk to you about just briefly is a document that you were shown by Ms. Mahindaratne at page 13699, and that would be D1095. Now, Mr. Turkalj, this is a daily combat report by the OG or the operation group Zadar, dated 4 August 1995. And as you see in the middle of the page that it has an insertion on paragraph 4 concerning the activities of the special police. Now, sir, I take it from your testimony that the orders you received to attack were different from the orders that the HV had given to Operation Group Zadar. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Concerning my or our orders, I issued orders to the group as for the targets that were supposed to be engaged, and they were not the same, yes. They were different to those of OG Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So OG Zadar had their own attack orders, and OG Zadar had their own target lists; and the special police had their attack orders, and the special police had their target lists. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I intended to bar table some attack order for OG Zadar as well as a target list and some supporting documentation, and at this point, and I discussed this with Mr. Russo, one of the documents I was told by the CLSS, they wouldn't translate -- I was told by Monday that they wouldn't translate one of the documents. This witness -- they have to do with OG Zadar. This is witness is a special policeman naturally, but I would ask the Court's intercession in assisting us in getting that last document translated, and I do believe Mr. Russo would concur in that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we -- if there is a translation issue, we have no problem with that. We asked to be a given a copy first of what was submitted to CLSS for translation to determine. I don't know if it is the whole document, what portions of it need to be translated. We just wanted to get a look at it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that the main purpose is to see who is in control of what kind of weaponry, and who would deploy it, under whose command it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a personal diary, Mr. President, without referring to the individual's name at this point. It's a personal diary that has a variety of information concerning the attack on the 4th and therefore and also some personal information, which is of no consequence. But I do believe the parties are interested in seeing that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is reasonable if you -- you're seeking the joinder of Mr. Russo in this exercise that you provide him with a copy, and then you will then have a joint enterprise it get it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think even with my good friend Mr. Russo's assistance, I still think we need to come back to you [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. If you want to bar table these documents, you know the guidance of the Chamber how to deal with that. Could I ask one additional question to Mr. Turkalj. Mr. Turkalj, I think you said - but let me check that first - that the Grad rockets were not used. Is that what you said? Let me just check it. Because they were not -- no replacement projectiles were ordered ... let me just find it. Yes. A question was put to you, Mr. Turkalj, saying: Now there is nothing in this list for the expenditure for rounds for a 122-millimetre Grad rocket system, is there? And then you said: No, it wasn't used. Did you mean it wasn't used at all, or wasn't used by you, or it was under someone else's control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that portion of the transcript in front of me. But the multiple rocket launcher Grad was used during Operation Storm, and there was a certain amount of ammunition that were expended, and that can be seen from the list of targets and ammunition spent in that area. But the issue of when it was used is a different matter and also which targets were engaged with this system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I just follow up on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to the replenishment of rounds for the 122, would that -- wouldn't that have come from the HV side and not be resupplied by the special police side?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think that the additional ammunition for the 122 system was not asked for, and I don't believe it arrived during Operation Storm itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift gears to the testimony that you had yesterday concerning the use of artillery for neutralizing and disruption. And I refer you back, Mr. President, to page 13704, beginning on line 11. You said: "Neutralizing it - 'it' meaning the target - means to make it impossible for these features to operate. Disrupting target means to fire a small number of projectiles upon that location in order to diminish its capacity to engage in the activities -- excuse me capacity to engage in the activities that location normally engages in." "Question: Judging from the tactics the artillery of the special police employed in the early stages of operation Storm, would you say that they engaged in -- that they engaged targets with a view to neutralizing them or disrupting their activity?" "Answer: Well, if we're talking about targets deep behind the line, then the exception was to disrupt their activity, whereas the targets that were on the front line or immediately behind the front line, then the intention was to neutralize the targets." Now, sir, I want to talk to you a little bit about your testimony about disrupting activity and where you note that you want to diminish the capacity to engage in activities that location normally engages in, and you also testified previously about shooting at cross-roads, cross-roads in depth; for instance, in Gracac. Talk to us a little bit about why you are shooting at cross-roads in depth and how that diminishes the capacity to engage in activities at that location.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I will try to be brief in my answer. One of the basic tasks of artillery is to prevent the introduction of new fresh forces to the front line where this is combat. As for intersections in the area of Gracac, they were of great importance for our axis of attack. Engaging that target as well as some other targets that had to do with roads contributed, in any case, to the forces that were supposed to be introduced to the -- into the combat area at the front line were made impossible to do that. That was one of our goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me just elaborate on that last answer a bit, and I know you want to keep this brief. But isn't a goal that you just discussed about artillery in depth and disrupting the activities of the ARSK designed to keep the ARSK in place and not gathering together and not moving around so they can come up to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, isn't one of the ways that artillery attempts to disrupt the activities in depth is to attempt to disrupt their communications by not allowing these various units to communicate or get together?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That is correct. It is another of the basic tasks of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about neutralisation of the enemy. And you talked about neutralizing the enemy. Not only at the front line but also behind the front line, just behind the front line. And that again is at 13704, lines 22 and 23. Can you explain that just a bit where you are trying to neutralize the target, the enemy, not only at the front line but behind the front line, what is that front line and what is the back -- the -- right behind the front line and how do they relate to one another?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: All the forces, including the army of the republic of the Krajina had its first line of defence. The front line. In my view, it's not 10 to 100 metres deep. It can be up to one kilometre deep, the first line of defence. Then every army would have its active duty forces, then reserve duty forces, and then the logistics at the rear. The task of the artillery is to neutralize all these forces along the first line of defence or the front line. You also have the command posts there of the units of the strength of companies, platoons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these were the targets when you're talking about neutralizing that you fired upon, beginning on the morning of the 4th. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Correct. These were the tasks that definitely had to be neutralized during the stage of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, I next would like to show you a document that I don't believe you have seen before, but it has been admitted into evidence and is a report from an ARSK colonel by the name of Jovan Kordic, and it is D435, and it is a report by the ARSK on the attack that ensued on the morning of the 4th by the special police. It's a five-page document in English in any event. I don't intend to go through it line by line. But if you can see, this is a report of the 9th Motorised Brigade of the ARSK. The 9th of August, 1995, where in the first paragraph they talk about the attack in the early morning. And the second paragraph: "Ustasha main forces mounted an attack with the focus on the region of defence of the 1st Motorised Battalion Mali Alan on 4 August 1995 at 0500. They were synchronizingly aiming at the town of Gracac and the road that leads from Gracac to Medak by long-range artillery with the focus on the Ruka crossing. That's the type of artillery attack that you're talking about that is attempting to disrupt the ARSK forces. Is that correct, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go down three paragraphs in that to despite extreme persistent defence and use of available forces and reserve, Ustasha forces managed to suppress our forces to the line of Mila Voda Pilar-Ruka-Medjuvode at 2100 hours with support of strong artillery and second echelon of special MUP, Ministry of Interior, MUP forces. If we can go to next the page. I'm going to ask you a couple of questions together going through this so we can move this more quickly. If you go to the next page, towards the bottom of page 2. "Considering the emerging situation on 5 August 1995 in the afternoon, when Knin and Korenica fell and there was a risk that the brigade could come under attack from the flank, following the order of the super ordinate command, we started an organised withdrawal of the brigade from the region of Ploce, Bruvno, Mazina, and on to the direction of Mazin, Dobro Sela, Petrovac in the evening hours. Along with the troops, the equipment was pulled out in an organised way. The greatest problem during the withdraw were the soldiers who went looking for their families; some of them found them and went straight to the federal republic of Yugoslav while others went to their villages to look for them. Loosing territory led to lowering morale, an interest for the defence, so no one but combat operations commanders and brigade command remained in Petrovac." Next page on the English. I'm not sure where it is on the -- it's on the same page. If go to the next page in the English, please, top of the page. "From the rear part of the brigade command remained no one but the technical service officer with an auto mechanic." Excuse me. "From the rear part of the brigade command remained no one by but the technical service officer with an auto mechanic. Dropping out was caused by not getting any information, decisions or commands from the superordinate command." Now, you noted for us earlier about the many uses of artillery and disrupting the efforts of the normal activities. Does one of the overall purposes in the use of artillery, especially in depth, is to turn the enemy forces, such as the ARSK into disarray, so soldiers abandon the front line, people leave the area, soldiers flee. Is that one of the intentions of the artillery use, especially in depth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I have already said that one of the main tasks and purposes of artillery is to disrupt and destroy communications centres so that the enemy side cannot engage in communication, which makes it difficult for them to maintain their flow of orders and commands. It made it easier for us to break their first line of defence and to advance in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one last couple of questions on this particular document, and I will complete -- I will be fished, Mr. Turkalj, and I would like just to go to the last page of this document, page 5, there's a conclusion. It says [indiscernible] -- that's correct. "As the main blow of the Ustasha attack was directed towards our brigade or more precisely to the 1st Motorised Brigade, where 55 troops went missing and 22 were wounded, the line of defence was broken, and with the fall of Knin and Korenica and massive evacuation of the people had started. With the approval of the super ordinate command, the brigade will to start organizing an evacuation. The evacuation of civilians, its own forces, and equipment was secured by the combat disposition." Now, Mr. Turkalj, prior to the events of Operation Storm, you had been involved in artillery attacks by the ARSK into Croatian-held territory; had you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That's correct. I was pretty familiar with the activity of the RSK artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when the RSK fired into Republic of Croatia territory or into Croatian-held territory, did -- what was the reaction of the civilian population in the -- in the Croatian-held territory? Did they flee, did they go into hiding? I mean, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: When the ARSK artillery fired upon targets or towns or civilian targets, I know that everyone sought refuge in shelters wherever they could. People did not abandon places where they lived, if that's what you're asking me about. They spent most of the time in shelters, and the situation -- such a situation prevailed for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's just talk about the attack on Gracac, and when you got to the Gracac, the Serb civilian population had evacuated, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. There was no civilian population in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, I mean based on your experience being on the other side of -- in Croatian-held territory receiving an artillery attack, were you surprised that, in fact, the entire civilian population had evacuated with the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President, what is the foundation this witness has not testified about being on the receiving line of artillery, and this is just a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the previous question was about how he experienced when --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How the civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the RSK fired into Republic of Croatia territory or in Croatian-held territory, what was the reaction of the civilian population? That was asked of the witness. That is what I understand receiving artillery, and now the comparison apparently is made between the reaction of the civilian population, as the witness experienced it before, being on the receiving side, and now on arriving at the side that had received the artillery from -- fired by the forces this witness was part of. That's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- could you please answer the question, Mr. Turkalj. Could you -- I think as a matter of fact, whether you were surprised or not is another matter. But I take it Mr. Kehoe wanted to know whether you saw similarities in the reaction of the civilian population you earlier had experienced where on Croatian-held territory artillery was fired at, compared to what you saw now, arriving in Gracac, where your artillery had fired at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take the liberty to answer Their Honours' question and the counsel 's question this way: I was surprised at the fact that there was no civilian population there. It was already said that the targets engaged in Gracac were engaged with an exceptionally small number of projectiles in view of the number of the targets in Gracac. To draw a comparison I was present in the area of the town of Karlovac where hundreds or even thousands of rounds landed on Karlovac, and the population never abandoned it. It was always there. So the movements of the population can never be correlated with the activities of shelling, or at least I could not when it came to the shelling of the towns that came from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Ms. Mahindaratne, could I first ask the witness to take off your earphones for a second. Ms. Mahindaratne, I told you that I would -- what happened yesterday is that you referred to a statement of this witness, then there was an objection by Mr. Kuzmanovic who objected against the line of questioning, saying that you had not asked Mr. Celic and that you should have done so. And then you reminded Mr. Kuzmanovic that if he would have read the statement by Mr. Celic, that he would have found that you had asked him, which is perfectly true. And then referring to the statement of this witness about the conversation he had in which he said, Well, I've done it, or whatever, and then you said, You'll find the statement of Mr. Celic, and in his testimony as well, that he refers to the conversation, and I'm now specifically pointing you to page 13664, lines 2 and 3, where you said: Where Drljo admits to burning of houses. Well, that's not what Mr. Celic said. It comes close to that. There is houses that were burned. It is Mr. Drljo who did not go around the village of Grubori but later admitted that he went through the village of Grubori, but there, Mr. Celic, does not tell us, as far as I can see, that in the conversation with Mr. Markac, the -- that he admits to burning of houses. Although a few lines later, it said that it was often, et cetera, but there's no admission strictly spoken from Mr. Drljo. That's what I would like to bring to your attention before you start your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I see your point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, you want to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that the Court -- what the court has just stated. I would just like to state on the record that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it appropriate to do it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Have the witness take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I have to ask you again to take off your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just think we need to be a little bit more circumspect when we accuse someone of making a frivolous objection. That's all I wanted to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that they are accepted, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, when you were just questioned by Mr. Kehoe, you said and this is at page 21, line 3, you said that one of the basic tasks of artillery is to prevent the introduction of new forces. Now, on Friday, when I asked you as to what targets you directed your artillery in Gracac, you identified three targets, and this is at transcript page reference 13585, line 11, you say, and I read that to you: "I'm talking about the brigade command, the 9th Gracac Brigade." Then you say: "Next there was a cross-roads in Gracac itself, the two main roads, and then there was a police station housing some of the operational forces in the area?" Those are the three targets you identified in Gracac that you used the artillery against. Now, what was the information that in these three military targets how many members of the ARSK were present at the time you decided to fire on those targets?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: It would be quite impossible to know the strength of the army at the time. We couldn't know exactly how many of them there were on the front line. Similarly we were unable to know how many of them there were in Gracac. When I spoke of the targets, I spoke of the military targets. Of course the brigade command is a military target. The police station is a military target. The cross-roads, of course, it is close to Gracac itself, and there were other targets as well around Gracac in depth. I also mentioned, if I remember well, the repeater, then Prezid which is a couple of kilometres away from Gracac. All of those were targets too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I couldn't, however, know how many soldiers were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, your testimony here is very specific. You identified three targets in Gracac, and -- okay. Let me ask you this way: Did you have information that there were members of the enemy forces present in the 9th Gracac Brigade command, at the time that you decided to fire on it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The information was that there was a brigade command there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is, did you have information that there were men in the command. There was a -- there were members of the SVK present, or have they left by this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, with all due respect. It's a headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I fully understand what is on your mind, but it is argumentative. Ms. Mahindaratne is asking a factual question, whether you would have put the same question to the witness is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne. You were asked whether you had any knowledge on whether this command was -- command post was -- I understand it that you want to know whether it was still active or whether it had been left by the -- by the forces who used -- who had this command post in use.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: This was the brigade command and such was the information. Weapon we're talking about the command of the brigade, we're not referring to room -- to a room or rooms. The command consists of a commander and members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have information you identified the second military target as a cross-roads in Gracac. Did you have information that the cross-roads were being, in fact, at the time used by enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: One of the tasks of the artillery was to prevent fresh forces from arriving and deploying on the front line. This can be done by firing upon the road. Even this very report by the commander, Mr. Kordic, makes it plain that this was precisely done. The roads were fired at, which prevented them from bringing in fresh forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you agreed when it was suggested to you by Mr. Mikulicic that the number of shells you may have fired on Gracac was approximately 15 shells. You agreed that that seemed to be an accurate reflection, and this is at transcript reference 13706, line 19, to 13707, line 6. Now, did you find that firing 15 rounds was sufficient to prevent new forces from arriving in Gracac? Is that the number of rounds that you would generally consider as being sufficient to prevent new forces from arriving?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I've already said that the objective was to disrupt. One could not prevent them fully from bringing in new forces, but one could disrupt them. The 15 shells you mentioned were the targets in Gracac, whereas the roads we fired at were in the general area of Gracac, and one could not tie the 15 shells with those, tie them in with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was that -- yesterday the second target that you identified, the cross-roads, you said, Cross-roads in Gracac itself, and this is at transcript reference number 13585, line 16. Your testimony, Mr. Turkalj, was that the cross-roads that you fired at were in Gracac itself. You used the word "itself." You said the two main roads. Now, are you saying in addition to that, there were other cross-roads that you fired at, or were you talking about that one particular cross-roads? Are you adding any further targets at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. You asked me about the targets located in the town of Gracac. The cross-roads you're referring to is in the general area of Gracac. It's not in downtown Gracac. The other targets I mentioned are not in Gracac. They are targets in elevated features, then the road between Ruka and Gracac which has nothing to with Gracac proper. I hope you understand now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on. Mr. Turkalj, yesterday you were asked about your artillery background by Mr. Mikulicic, and this is at T13696, line 10. You said that you have specialized in artillery. Can you describe to the Chamber what kind of training have you received in artillery, in terms of years, what type of training, what type of courses you have taken.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, I went through all the training for artillery I could possibly have done. I graduated from the Military Academy, and then I worked for some three more years in the JNA and in the HV thereafter, always in the field of artillery. When it comes to our army, that as much training as one could possibly obtain in the field of artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction not the HV but the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you say in terms of specific training in artillery, how many years have you spent in training?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I graduated from the Military Academy and was a JNA officer holding the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And as a JNA officer, were you involved in -- in artillery unit, or were you commanding artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I was a battery commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. The witness was asked a question at line 22 on page 33, Can you say in terms of specific training, how many years have you spent in training? And then I believe he was answering on his period of time in the Military Academy, and I believe that Counsel went into other question without an answer to that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently Ms. Mahindaratne was satisfied by the answer. Do I understand, Mr. Turkalj, that apart from your Military Academy training, that you were trained constantly on the job, both in the JNA and later when you worked in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Military Academy, I specialised in the artillery. That is to say I graduated from the military academy as a specialist in artillery. After that, I spent another three years as a JNA officer. After that, I moved to the Ministry of Interior; that is to say, the police. As you can see from my previous statement, I worked in the police specifically with regards to artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you not take any additional courses after you had left the Military Academy, in artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of regular duties in the army, there are additional courses and checks of each and every single officer, including myself. There is live ammunition, exercise, blanks being used for exercise. That is part of the regular work in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Moving on to another area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before you do so, I'm looking at the clock. It's 10.30. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just need about two or three minutes. I have only two questions more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I will allow you to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified that although Mr. Drljo did not submit a written report that he informed you that -- that he was not present, and he did not know what happened in Grubori on 25th August. Let me take you, Mr. Turkalj, and you also said that you did not consider his failure to submit one report as a reason to seek disciplinary measures against him. This testimony at page number 13676, line 20, and transcript page number 13681, line 22, going to 13628, line 4. Now, let me read back to you your testimony so far on the issue of Mr. Drljo and his failure to submit a report. If I could ask to you look at your 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, may I have your assistance. That is P1149. There's a binder of hard copies which were handed over to the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be behind tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It should be behind tab 1, but I don't think he has been given. If I could have on the screen P1149, Mr. Registrar. And if we could move to paragraph 61. Also in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljo [sic], if you could read paragraph 61, this is what you say: "Franjo Drljo was not disciplined for refusing to submit a report, and although Mr. Celic, Mr. Curkovic, and myself asked General Markac for him to be removed from the Lucko Unit, this was not done."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Ms. Mahindaratne. Could the counsel please take in mind remarks on that count that were made by the witness on the beginning of direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first read it and then pay attention to further observations made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You go on to say this: "... and this was not done. The three of us had on more than one occasion discussed with Mladen Markac the problem of trying to manage Drljo who was a problem before the Grubori incident, and, in fact, before Operation Storm. Both Markac and Sacic were well aware of the problem we were having with Drljo." And on page 63 you say: "Drljo was a difficult man to command in the field. He was very nationalistic but was always, in my opinion, very careful about his behaviour when a superior was around. utterances.text: Could someone remind me exactly where the witness made, so that I can read it. It's about paragraph 61. Mr. Mikulicic, could you give me the ...

utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, your testimony here is you did not consider it necessary to take disciplinary measures against Mr. Drljo for that one failure to submit a written report, but your testimony here yesterday was that -- that was his -- your testimony, whereas your testimony according to the statement given so far is that you had, in fact, not only you, two others had asked Mr. Markac to remove Drljo from the Lucko Unit, which is quite different to what you said yesterday. utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I have not changed my statement, at least not in full. On the other hand, Mr. Drljo was an exceptional fighter. He was of much use to the special police. I thought that a single report or a disciplinary procedure that may effect five per cent of his net salary symbolic, a fine wouldn't change much as regards his relationships towards discipline and relationship to his superiors. That is what I did not ask for him to be sanctioned. However, I do believe he would have been happier if he had been sent elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I did not have any information of Mr. Drljo committing anything bad, any criminal offence. The only issue at hand was the one of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, how is it that you did not mention that Mr. Drljo verbally told you that he did not know anything that happened in Grubori, either in your statement when you were interviewed in 2004 or in 2005, which was video-recorded. How is it that you said it for the first time here in court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I must confess that after so many years, it is difficult to remember every detail. I believe you have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. I think the observation was made at page 13545 that the witness corrected or at least gave further information about paragraph 61 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, when you received this -- this phone call from Mr. Sacic when you were still in Zagreb, I would like to know a few more details about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember where you exactly were at that time? That's the phone call you received before you went to Gracac and then to the Plavno area, Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely where I was at that moment. In any case, I was in the area of Zagreb. I can't tell you decidedly where I was when I received the phone call, in what part of the city I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that it may have been at home. Is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No. It was an aside. I did say I may have been at home. I'm sorry if I gave you the impression that I was there indeed. I merely wanted to say that I could have been anywhere in Zagreb. I can't tell you anything more precisely than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly did Mr. Sacic tell you during this telephone conversation, about the reason for which he asked you to come to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
