utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't ask him what kind of event you were invited for to travel quite a distance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I understand that he called you the day before you actually left for Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think that phone call took place late in the afternoon, or early evening of the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time that Mr. Celic was also invited to join?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I was not. When I received the phone call, I asked the unit duty officer to put me through to Mr. Celic. I told him that he should be in the area of Gracac the next morning as well, so that we could go to Plavno together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you'd travelled on your own. Did you use your private car or ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was alone in an official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Celic, did you use an official vehicle as well, or did he use a private vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: He used an official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the reason, if you go to the same destination, both being on duty, to use separate official vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I had things to do afterwards in the area that I hail from - that is, Slunj - after the visit. We simply decided to meet up in the area of Gracac. I was the one to ask for that, because I didn't know where Plavno was exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any -- is there any further need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, this finishes your examination. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long distance to The Hague and for having answered the questions put to you by the parties and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, while we have a break anyhow. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, before we continue, the Chamber would like to give an oral decision on a pending motion, which is unrelated to the next witness. The Chamber will now deliver its decision on the Prosecution's motion to admit 93 HV artillery documents into evidence and to add 36 of these to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Chamber would also like to provide some related guidance to the parties. The Prosecution filed its motion on the 18th of November, 2008. On the 21st of November, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion to bar the Prosecution from adding the 36 HV artillery documents to the Rule 65 ter list. On the 24th of November, the Markac Defence joined the submission of the Gotovina Defence. On the following day, the Prosecution filed a request for leave to reply to the Gotovina Defence's motion, which it deemed to be a response to its motion. On the 26th of November, the Chamber decided to grant the Prosecution's request for leave to reply and informed the parties accordingly, through an informal communication. The Chamber found that, although formally named a motion, the filing of the Gotovina Defence amounted in substance to a response to the Prosecution's motion. On the 28th of November, the Prosecution filed a reply. On the 2nd of December, the Gotovina Defence filed a second response, objecting to the admission into evidence of certain HV artillery documents. The Chamber accepts in this instance the filing of two response, each addressing one aspect of the Prosecution's motion, and jointly exceeding the word limit of 3.000 words, but instructs the parties that in the future, they should file no more than one response each to any motion, and not exceed the word limit without seeking authorisation and showing exceptional circumstances, as set out in points 5 and 7 of the practice direction on the length of briefs and motions of the 16th of September, 2005. On the 5th of December, the Prosecution requested leave to reply to Gotovina's second response. On the same day, the Chamber decided to grant the request and informed the parties accordingly, through an informal communication. On the 9th of December, the Prosecution filed a reply. On the 10th of December, the Gotovina Defence requested leave to sur-reply to this reply. On the same day, the Chamber gave each party two minutes for final submissions which can be found at transcript pages 13536 to 13538. Appendix A to the Prosecution's motion provides short descriptions of the content of the tendered documents, which indicate that they are of a technical nature. For instance, document number 63, which, among others, was not provided in the motion, is described as a, and I quote, "artillery expenditure report of the 7th Home Guard Regiment." The Chamber reiterates that documents should preferably be tendered for admission through witnesses who are able to comment on them. This allows for proper contextualization without which the Chamber is left to determine relevance and probative value primarily on the basis of the documents alone. These considerations are especially pertinent for documents of a technical nature such as those as described in Appendix A, for which the relevance and probative value is not immediately apparent. Appendix A contains a brief description of the relevance of each tendered document. However, in several instances, this description appears to be truncated. Furthermore, the descriptions are generally insufficient to clarify for the Chamber the probative value and relevance of each specific document in relation to the indictment and other evidence. For instance, the relevance of document 63 in Appendix A is merely described as, I quote, "expenditure of artillery during 4th August 1995, including 155 MBRL 128-millimetre rockets." Document 89, which was provided under number 32 in Appendix B to the motion contains a multitude of technical details, including 13 pages of firing tables for the RAK 128-millimetre multiple rocket launcher. Neither its relevance nor its probative value is clear on the face of the document. For these reasons, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's motion in its entirety, without prejudice. In case the Prosecution would seek to tender these documents into evidence again, it should remove any documents that have already been admitted into evidence and make a careful selection of the remaining ones based on their importance to the case. The Chamber would then strongly encourage the Prosecution to tender them through a witness who could provide the Chamber with the proper contextualization. For any document not on the Rule 65 ter list, the Chamber instructs the Prosecution to announce this before putting the document to the witness. The Chamber would then hear the parties on questions such as when that individual document was obtained by the Prosecution; when and how it was disclosed to the Defence; its relevance and probative value; and what burden, if any, its addition would place on the Defence, before deciding whether it may be added to the Rule 65 ter list and put to the witness. If the Prosecution would nevertheless deem it necessary to exceptionally tender from the bar table any remaining documents, the Chamber would expect the Prosecution to do so in limited numbers. The Prosecution should provide for each document information about its content, its relevance to the indictment, its importance in light of other evidence, along with references to the relevant portions of any long documents. The Prosecution should also notify the Chamber and the Defence of each document that is not on the Rule 65 ter list, and indicate when that document came into the possession of the Prosecution, and when and how it was disclosed to the Defence. This concludes the Chamber's decision and guidance. Mr. Russo, I was informed that you wanted to raise certain matters before you call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I thought we could address some of the objections to the documents I had intended to tender across the bar table during or at the conclusion of the witness's evidence. Some of them, in fact, I will be using or may be using. I was informed last night because of some of the options from the Defence. I thought we could hear those first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me be quite frank to you I didn't give any follow-up this morning to what happened yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could just state that my -- I made some objections last night in preparing for this witness's testimony so my objections, indeed, were a little bit late both to Mr. Russo and to the Chamber, and I apologise for that. There are three documents that I do have some objections to. Basically it's the same objection which is that some of the reports either in whole or in substantial part discuss incidents that occur technically speaking within Sector South, but the Prosecution agrees that they occurred neither in the Split Military District nor in the Knin municipality. They occur in the -- in the northern-most area of Sector South which would be in the Gospic Military District. My concern with admission of the documents. For -- I would argue that they have no probative value, but even if there was an argument that they have limited probative value is that -- my concern is that when the Chamber is reviewing these documents at a later date, it may be difficult just going by village names for the Chamber to keep distinct which of these villages falls within which Military District, and for that reason I raised with Mr. Russo my concern about admitting those documents in evidence I understand that Mr. Russo is prepared to stipulate on behalf of the Prosecution that with respect to those documents that those areas fall outside the Split Military District and outside the Knin municipality. Nevertheless, I still wanted to raise it with the Chamber because I'm still not sure of the relevance to the issues in this trial, and also I don't know as a matter of housekeeping whether the Chamber wanted to make a decision on how easy it will be later to keep in mind that these areas are in the Split Military District. So the exhibits I lodged an objection to are 65 ter 4125, 65 ter 4133, and 65 ter 4252. Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, we join in those objections as well, with regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Join in those objections. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may, I'm sorry, Mr. Russo. I see on the transcript it says, I want to make sure that I have the right exhibits. It's 65 ter 4125 and not 65 ter 4135, as is currently reflected on the transcript. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if you want to hear from me with respect to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that there are three issues. The first being the objection itself, that it is irrelevant and without probative value. The second is how to identify what documents are, although in Sector South and I would say in the -- the relevant Military Districts. And then the third one whether the Chamber wants to make up its own mind, of course, the Chamber wants, but often follows suggestions given by the parties. Now as far as the first one is, it's on the record. The second one, I take it, that you you'll work that out, and that we'll receive further details as this is at that location is not within the Split Military District and outside the Knin municipality, so that's a technical matter as well. The third one, I think that the Chamber would like to have a look at them and to see whether we finally are satisfied with the further explanations and then admit them, or not to add met them at all. But from what I understand, these documents as such, that's how I understood your objection, Mr. Misetic, do not really harm at this very moment -- so therefore that we can take our time because you say irrelevant, lack of probative value, but it is not unfair to the Defence or something like that at this moment, apart from being without probative value and being without sufficient relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Completely correct. I would only add that our concern really would only arises that if these documents are admitted into evidence and then later on it becomes -- I'm just concerned that we could start to confuse issues, and if they are admitted, that it should be somehow very clear these are outside the relevant Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that we need only a yellow marker on them, but it should be purple and all that in order to avoid that the Chamber may make a mistake -- may make the mistake that these are within the relevant geographical scope and technical scope of the indictment. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if you recall William Hayden's testimony, we had a similar time of redaction for several exhibits or at least one exhibit in that case, similar situation, sort of outside of the sector of the portion the indictment. That's really what we're focussed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which immediately triggers an invitation to the parties whether they could resolve the matter. But if you disagree, Mr. Russo, and, of course, you have not expressed your views on the relevance and the probative value, which might be, for you, a reason not to -- not to enter into any further discussions on this matter with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I did provide these documents to the Defence several weeks ago indicating the areas which we believed were relevant. That discussion ended in no agreement with respect to what could be submit to the chamber, with respect to what portions of the document the Court should pay attention to. So I'm not sure -- I'm certainly willing to give it a try. We can certainly agree with respect to the paragraphs in these particular reports which deal with matters outside of the Split Military District. I do believe it is distinct from the situation which Mr. Kuzmanovic mentions, not outside the sector simply out the Split Military District. I think there is an important distinction to be made there. Also with respect to the argument that they're not relevant because they're not in the Split Military District, we would certainly not agree with that. It is a JCE we have alleged. The conduct of HV soldiers occurring immediately outside of the Split Military District is also relevant to a pattern of conduct by HV soldiers, the widespread nature of the incidents, and also the likelihood of notice to the higher commanders of what was happening in the area. That's our basis for putting forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore if the Chamber receives -- of course, the documents are tendered into evidence, we'll then receive notice from both parties which paragraphs are as far as the Defence is concerned without probative value and without relevance, and for you, still relevant and of probative value, but outside the Split Military District area and outside Knin. Then we also know what to focus on, if deciding -- when determining what should or what should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond just briefly to Mr. Russo' comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two points. One is that with respect to his suppositions on the relevance, under that argument then, all matters that took place in Sector North would also be admissible into evidence here. And given the Chamber's prior ruling concerning Mr. Hayden and when he was here, I don't believe that that -- admitting these documents for that purpose would be consistent with excluding documents that -- concerning events that took place in Sector North. And secondly, it is our position, Your Honour, that Sector South as a term is an UN term. It is not a legal or a geographic term within the Croatian structures, and therefore, the fact that something occurred in Sector South within an UN boundary but not within -- within any Military District or civilian district relevant to this indictment, I don't think has any bearing on the matters before the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. These incidents which are discussed in these documents are -- occurred in areas which were under the original indictment. It was upon the Chamber's invitation to limit the scope of the indictment that these areas were cut out. So it is not as if they are expanded beyond original indictment area and I believe physical location as we can agree on to the locus of other crimes which were committed within the indictment area certainly makes it more relevant as opposed to if they happened 50 kilometres north of that area. And to be clear, Your Honour, the Court's decision 21 February 2007 on our motion to cut the indictment down, the Court did note our position with respect to the relevance of this kind of conduct for pattern, intent, motive evidence, and I believe the Court approved of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to make one additional point in light of that. Patterns, motive, course of conduct has some relevance if we're talking one of the three defendants in this case. Pattern evidence of what somebody else was doing in a different Military District, I think has very low probative value and especially when compared to how much of that evidence could then come in under -- through that door. I would ask that the Chamber exclude this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think submissions are sufficient for the Chamber to decide the matter, unless, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing on the substance, more on the procedure, Your Honour. And we appreciate the fact that we did receive the bar table submission on November 28th, but the Chamber should be aware that the bar table submission had been changed twice the last time last night, either adding or taking documents away in addition to the exhibit list, so we're trying to get the documents and make our objections known as quickly as possible. But in this case the last admission we had on the bar table was yesterday at 3.30 or so in the afternoon, so we're doing our best to keep up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not comment on this last one. Mr. Russo, I think on the substance we have heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. We're prepared to call our next witness, Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi, witness 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Al-Alfi. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, you're not a native English-speaking person. If you ever have any problems in expressing yourself or in understanding my English or the English of any of the other persons here, please ask me for clarification so that we don't have any confusion. Mr. Al-Alfi, you will first be examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.text: My name is Hussein Al-Alfi. It is H-u-s-s-e-i-n, Al-Alfi, A-l - A-l-f-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall giving a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor on 5 March 1998?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 6493. Mr. Al-Alfi, I'll ask you to please pause between my question and your answer, and I will do the same. We have several translators working at once. Mr. Al-Alfi, if you could please have a look at the screen in front of you, and I will ask Mr. Registrar to please move this to the second page. utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO

utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.text: In the page 26, at the last line, there were some who were called in the transcript, who were caught, in the city, not cold, that means stranded in the city; they could not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Caught?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Caught, yes, that is what I'm saying. Not cold. Sorry, just bear with me, I'm just trying to ... On page 38 in the middle of it, it said I used to accompany General Cermak to all meetings.
