utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Al-Alfi, given those corrections that you made, does the statement accurately reflect what you told the investigator on 5 March 1998?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were asked those same questions here today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were the answers you gave, and is the information in that statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that basis, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 6493.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P1160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1160 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have the assistance of the court usher, I have a clean copy of the witness's statement plus some of the Exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, you can use this to refer to some of the documents I'm going to be showing you during your examination. And with the Chamber's permission, I would like to read a brief summary of the witness's 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Al-Alfi aware of the purpose of this exercise? He may not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't believe he is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, Mr. Russo will read a summary of your statement. That is it not evidence, but for the public to be able to follow these proceedings. Written statements, of course, do not inform the public. So therefore, what he reads is a summary of what is in your statement, but the statement itself is the evidence, not the summary. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi was the civil affairs coordinator for the former UN Sector South from June of 1995 until January of 1996, although his official title changed to political and humanitarian affairs coordinator after the fall of Knin. This was the highest UN civilian representative position in the Knin area. Mr. Al-Alfi was present in Knin during the artillery attack on 4 and 5 August 1995, and described it as massive, indiscriminate, and a shelling of the whole town. Mr. Al-Alfi stated that after the fall of Knin, the area was mostly under military rule and that General Cermak was the military commander in charge of Knin and its suburbs. Mr. Al-Alfi met with General Cermak on several occasions to advise General Cermak of the killings, lootings, burnings and other human rights violations occurring in the area and that these crimes were often perpetrated by or in the presence of Croatian soldiers. General Cermak sometimes denied that those responsible were Croatian soldiers but also made assurances that this conduct would be stopped. Mr. Al-Alfi met with the mayor of Knin and described those meetings as a waste of time, because the mayor would refer Mr. Al-Alfi to General Cermak or state that he himself would address the issue with General Cermak. Mr. Al-Alfi stated that General Cermak was the only authority in the area to whom Mr. Al-Alfi could address concerns about the human rights violations which were being reported. That concludes my summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Please forgive me, Mr. Al-Alfi, if I pause for too long. We have the French translation to catch up with.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Al-Alfi, can you please inform the Chamber as to what specifically were your duties and responsibilities as the political and humanitarian affairs coordinator?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: I was assigned or reassigned to Sector South, and if I may pause with your permission to say how this is an administrative division of the UN into sectors, Sector South, Sector West, Sector North, but in the Vance -- and Sector East, four sectors we had. But in the Vance Plan which created the United Nations protected areas, you will see that there are three UNPAs. Three United Nations protected areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, the Chamber is well aware of -- I do understand you are not aware of what the Chamber knows, but if you focus on Mr. Russo' question, because sectors, et cetera, we hear in this case for quite a while, so we are quite familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I apologise for interrupting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the reassigned as the highest civilian. First, I was reassigned as civil affairs coordinator, and later on, that post was changed to be political and humanitarian affairs coordinator and in charge of the whole sector of civilian matters of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And as part of your duties, were you required to sent reports to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course. I had staff under me who were called civil affairs officers, and later on, renamed as political and humanitarian affairs officers, and we had the Human Rights Action Teams who came to work for that purpose after the fall of the sector. And all of them, some of them are directly reporting to me, then I convey my own reports to the headquarters. Sometimes I transmitted the whole report as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Chamber an idea of what kind of information you would write reports on. What was the substance matter of these reports?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: As I said, based on the reports I received from my civil affairs officers mainly and sometimes by receiving a copy of the reports submitted by the Human Rights Action Teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did these reports include information regarding human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Al-Alfi, if we could -- first let me ask you, if you could please tell the Chamber where you were on the morning of the artillery attack on Knin.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: I was in my house in Knin, not far from our headquarters. Around 3.30, 4.00, early in the morning, I received a call from my headquarters telling me that they received information from our headquarters in Zagreb, that the zero hour will be at 5.00, and they were coming to pick me up from my house. They came and picked me up from my house, and I went to our headquarters in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you could please just briefly describe for the Chamber what you saw and heard of the artillery attack on the first day.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: It was -- it was a massive artillery. Definitely according to our military, it was from a distance, and we could hear the bombing all over the place. In some areas, we could see the impact of those bombings, and we could see even some of the houses burning but from our headquarters, seeing through the windows to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you personally observe some of this yourself?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: What do you mean by "observe"? Observing firing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Observe the impacts in the town.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes. From a distance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Chamber whether houses, civilian houses, were hit from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes. The areas which were hit were civilian --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would first allow the witness to finish his answer. Could you complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Because we know the area. We had been in the area at least -- by then I was there for almost three months. And from our side of the headquarters, we could see some of the areas hit, not only houses, water tanks, electricity plants, and all that, we could see them that they are on fire, and the hit is on that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you have observed Mr. Misetic's request if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- want to further explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, can you please tell the Chamber from what vantage point were you looking into the city of Knin?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, I was in my office, and we had windows that you can see parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in some of the areas where you saw impacts landing, how did you know that they were civilian houses, for example?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: As I said, we were in that area for two, three months before that, I was there, and where it lands is a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you give the Chamber some idea of how long the artillery attack went on for on the first day?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: On the first day, it was almost continuous, and it was heavy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And briefly again, if you could describe your observations of the shelling which occurred on the following day.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: On the following day, it was to a lesser extent from the first day. Mostly much lesser than what it was on the first day. And one -- some of those areas even hit as far as I recall, and we saw it on fire. That was a direct hit, which used to be the radio station of the -- the Knin -- in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Chamber when was the first time that you left the UN compound after the artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, as I said in my statement, for the day -- for the first day, second day, we could not go out of our compound at all, because we only realized when there were two tanks outside our compound from the Croatian army, outside our compound, not allowing even our military to move out. And there was an agreement worked between the special representative in Zagreb, Mr. Akashi and the government, which we knew about it later even, as a copy of it, that they would allow us freedom of movement. So if I'm not mistaken, around the 8th or the 9th, we were allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you accompany Mr. Akashi when he came to Knin?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, yes, I'm the one who received him at the heli-port.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you accompany him into the town itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Chamber what you witnessed inside the town of Knin on that day?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Although it was the fourth or fifth day almost of the operation, there were still at that time at least -- we observed at least 10 or 11 houses on fire in town, and we saw destruction, either some houses already burnt or some damages to other houses, and many of the houses even the doors were open. And we saw some vehicles around, some civilian, some military, and loaded with looted things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you personally witness items being looted from houses?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Not seeing them in action, but I saw the looted items.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I see. And these looted items, were they in the possession of the civilians or of military personnel?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Both of them. Sometimes military, or military trucks even, and sometimes on civilian cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Chamber an idea of what you mean when you say looted items. What exactly kind of items are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, sometimes you see TV, you see radio, you see clothes, whatever, personal belongings in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you had mentioned that there were civilians participating in this. Do you know how those civilians arrived in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: I don't know how exactly, but they had Croatian plate numbers, which are plate numbers in Croatia proper at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And at the time that Mr. Akashi had come to the UN -- I mean, to Knin, was -- were the military personnel from the UN allowed freedom of movement at that time, or did it come later?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: At that time, the agreement was already reached in Zagreb, and on paper, yes, it says freedom of movement, but it was not -- in actual practice, it was not full freedom of movement. I mean, some areas, we were not allowed to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And after the Croatian forces had taken control over the area, who became your official point of contact in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: You mean in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber approximately when the first time you met General Cermak was, and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, the first or second day after we were allowed to leave our compound. And it was accompanying General Forand, because now it is a military situation. Our military meets with their military, and I was accompanying General Forand as his advisor in the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you mentioned General Forand being present. Can you tell the Chamber who, if anyone else, you recall being present at that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: General Forand always -- not always, in many times when he goes for such meetings, he is accompanied by the Chief of Staff Colonel Leslie, a Canadian also, our Chief of Staff. And from the other side, there were some people. I don't recall them. But there were always two military people attending the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber whether anyone from the UN side present at the meeting informed General Cermak about what was happening, some of the things you just mentioned occurring in Knin, the burning houses and the looting?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, from the first minute we saw General Cermak, we were all officials including me. We were stressing that point: You have to stop what's going on in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you inform the Chamber as to General Cermak's response to this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course. The first reaction, either I don't know about it, or I will make sure that nothing happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what your understanding was of Mr. Cermak's -- my apologies, General Cermak's authority in the area.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, to me, he was the highest military commander in Knin and the suburbs, and if I recall correctly, this was even transmitted to our headquarters officially, that he is officially appointed as the military commander or military governor of Knin and the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did General Cermak ever indicate to you that he was without authority to stop the events that you were witnessing and reporting to him?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you please explain to the Chamber how exactly you communicated with General Cermak. Was it through an UN interpreter, or was it through an interpreter of General Cermak's?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: At that time we did not have interpreters with us, so it was through his own interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And going back to what General Cermak had told you regarding what was happening and what was being reported to you, did he ever indicate to you that he did not have the ability to stop what was happening?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: He did not at all, because if he start saying like that, then why is he there, the question would be raised. But he said, I will stop and sometimes he even was instructing some of his people to go and see those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And were you present when he was issuing orders as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: I could -- I did not understand the language, but I could see that he is taking action, and immediately he is calling someone, and he is mentioning the same areas that I am mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you a report about your first meeting with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 4756.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will appear on your screen, Mr. Al-Alfi, and perhaps you can also use the hard copy. Mr. Russo will tell you to find it behind which tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It should be behind the second tab in the binder which was given to you, if you prefer the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I prefer. Number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Second tab, it's the report dated 8 August at 1640 hours. Mr. Registrar, if we could move the screen in English, just up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, do you recognise your signature in the "from box" on this report?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now if we could go to the first paragraph. In the second sentence, you state: "We were informed by General Cermak, the military governor in the area, that the Croatian army started to pull out of the main cities, including Knin. This is true in Knin where more military and civilian police are seen in the streets, rather than military personnel." Now, Mr. Al-Alfi, can you tell the Chamber whether this particular observation was one which you made personally or was this reported to you by someone else?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: It was reported to me by all my civil affairs officers also. And it could have been observed also, because we started moving a little bit in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to admit 65 ter 4756.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P1161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1161 is admitted into evidence. In the absence of any objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Al-Alfi, that report was dated 8th of August, 1995. I would like to compare it now with a subsequent report you made ten days later, on the 18th of August, and I believe this will appear in the tab number 6. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 4101.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Did you say number 6? 12th or 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, it should be -- 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yeah, here 18th. It should be number 7, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, number 7. Now if we go to first paragraph in the fourth sentence, where you state: "Some of the military manifestations are being moved out of Knin, and some still remain in the area. More military and civilian police are being brought to replace the soldiers. The local Croatian civilian authorities justify this slow normalisation by a 'surprise quick victory' in the military offensive." Mr. Al-Alfi, can you please clarify for the Chamber whether there was still a significant presence of military soldiers and not just policemen or military policemen on the 18th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, we have to understand that it was a military operation and when we say the military had been withdrawn, that does not mean every single one. That means there will be some movement, and there was still some movement, but they were not as intensive as they used to be in the beginning. That's what I meant by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you also clarify the statement by these Croatian officials that this slow normalisation was the result of a surprise quick victory. Can you tell the Chamber, from your perspective, why or if they explained to you why a surprise quick victory resulted in the slow removal of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, I believe the belief which was prevailing at the time maybe even for the Croatian authorities, that there would be a longer resistance from the Serbs who were in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Russo' question accurately states what the report says. I can see reference to slow normalisation, not slow removal of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you're invited to quote literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps can I clarify with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long the quote is still accurate. If you rely on the quote. If not, then make that clear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could respond to the objection first. The line, the local Croatian authorities justified this slow normalization as a descriptor of the previous sentence which indicates that soldiers are still remaining in the area and [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the general guidance is that if there's any objection against way in witch a document is presented to a witness that that should be immediately stopped, and then by putting it to literally to the witness, if you need two sentences for that, then read two sentences, but let's not start interpreting the document in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, in the sentence where you say: The local Croatian civilian authorities justify this slow normalization by a surprise quick victory in the military offensive," what did you mean when you refer to "this slow normalization"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: If you see the two sentences or three sentences before this statement, it is very clear we're talking about normalization for one reason. We are not talking about the military. We are talking about restoring water and electricity and all this, that's why I say slow normalization.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would move to admit 65 ter 4101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1162 is admitted into evidence, in the absence of any objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, may I also, looking at the clock either now or within the next two or three minutes, could you find a suitable moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now is just as good as any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Al-Alfi, we'll have a break of approximately 20 minutes. We resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I'm usually not commenting on ... And neither do I today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could please have P1161.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, if I could take you back to tab 2 in your folder, this is, again, the 8th August report that we had discussed a bit earlier. And if we could go to paragraph 5 of that document, which I believe is on the second page. And you can see there, Mr. Al-Alfi, in paragraph 5, it indicates: "According to General Cermak, the Croatian civilian authorities are expected to arrive in Knin today?" Mr. Al-Alfi, were you aware of an announcement that civilian authority had been restored prior to this meeting you had with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in your view, from dealing with General Cermak and with others, did it appear to you that civilian authority had been restored in Knin when you first met with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And also in that paragraph the third sentence, you mention that General Cermak had promised to arrange a meeting between you and these civilian authorities for that same afternoon. Can you tell the Chamber how long it was until you actually got a meeting with the civilian authorities in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No meeting was held. He only promised it, but there was no meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if Mr. Russo -- at what point he will be done with this line of questioning, but I would note an objection to the foundation for the earlier questions about, Did it appear to you. I think it is unclear as to the basis for how one would arrive such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Mr. Russo, whether you want to explore that or whether we leave it to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe it may become clear on further questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait and see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Al-Alfi, did you, in fact -- at some later point, were you introduced to other people who were in civilian authority in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Only one, who was appointed like the mayor of Knin or something like that. I think if I'm not mistaken his name was Relic [phoen], but it is mentioned in one of my reports. I don't recall the full name correctly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And this mayor of Knin that you mention, can you tell the Chamber what kinds of things you met with him about?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Because I was dealing with the civilian side, so for me, it is appropriate to deal with the civilian side, who was supposedly to be the mayor. So I started -- I had one or two meetings in the beginning with him, but I found that he had no answers except to receive the [indiscernible], and in some occasions he even told me, It's better you deal with it on these issues with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Chamber an idea of what kinds of issues he asked to you address with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course. They were like cases reported to me by my civil affairs officers about some people suffering intimidation or something like that on the civilian side, and I would go to him, because this is a civilian matter now, and he would say, I cannot do anything at this point. It's better to take it with General Cermak. Because he knew also that I still had the contact with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, go back to General Cermak with those concerns?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, again, can you tell the Chamber what General Cermak's response was when you continued to bring him this information?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: He would take them. He would take them, and he said, I will look into it, or I will see what I can do. But in some cases, yes, we saw some change; in other cases, the same situation continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, when you say suffering, intimidation, or something like that, what kind of suffering did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some areas, sir, when it used to be reported to me that people are afraid even to go to their houses back, and they were even living in the mountains because they were afraid, and they are civilians. Because of the movement of Croatian army in those hamlets. That is what I meant by suffering and intimidation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You take them together. It's not suffering something separate from intimidation because you can imagine suffering without intimidation. But you took them together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, you mentioned that some of the things that you brought to General Cermak's attention that you said afterwards you saw some change in some cases. Can you please give the Chamber some information about what it was that changed after you notified General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: In fact, there are two things in this issue. Sometimes if you brought to his attention that was some houses burning, by the time he comes back, the burning is done, the damage is done, so there is no more to be burnt, or some houses will still being looted. So everything is done already. When I get the response, that means everything is already done. Everything is okay. Okay, but in what status? Other things, when I went to him, and I said, The people of this hamlet or -- it was reported to me that they are afraid, he would give instructions to some of his colleagues around to go and check into that hamlet immediately. And the second day, I would send my own people again, and I would find that people are saying, We are okay, no one is intimidating us anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did the civil affairs officers that you had sent to areas like that, did they confirm to you that, in fact, General Cermak had indeed sent people or that people had showed up at General Cermak's request?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: They confirmed to me only one thing, that from the people, they knew that some people appeared there. But they did not say whether General Cermak or not. I guessed at that, because I talked to General Cermak earlier about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move to paragraph 7 of this report, I just want to ask one question on a slightly unrelated issue. In paragraph 7, you indicate in the third sentence that someone from the Croatian Red Cross had informed you that all of the draft-age males of the displaced persons in the UN compound were prisoners of war. Can you clarify for the Chamber whether this person from the Croatian Red Cross was telling you -- can you clarify why they were telling that these were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Because, according to our information from our civil affairs officers, we knew that they took some people, that they came into the sector, outside what used to be the sector, to what used to be called proper Croatia. And this man from the Croatian Red Cross in Zadar confirmed that, to them, they are prisoner of war, especially those who were in military uniform of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by your answer. Paragraph 7 indicates that, quote: "Mr. Branko Zubovic from the Croatian Red Cross in Zadar asked for a list of displaced persons inside Sector South headquarters. According to him this request is made on behalf of the Croatian government. He claimed that those displaced persons who were males much draft age are prisoners of war." Can you clarify whether Mr. Brankovic [sic] is referring to people who -- the displaced persons inside of the UN compound or displaced persons elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: He is talking about the displaced persons inside the compound, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you whether the decision to designate them as prisoners of war was his own, or was this on behalf of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, he was saying according to the Croatian government, but I did not go further to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It indicates after that sentence: "He further informed us that there are 300 Serb prisoners in Zadar, out of whom 50 to 100 are military." Did he explain to you why the other 150 to 200 people apparently who were not military were being held as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to -- Mr. Registrar, please, 65 ter 4134. And, Mr. Al-Alfi, this report dated 24 August appears at tab 9. And if we could move to the last page. Mr. Al-Alfi, this report covers some observations of a Human Rights Action Team from Vrlika to Knin reporting looting and destruction. And in the last page, the third sentence of the second-to-last paragraph. And the sentence I'm interested in is: "The continuation of houses destroyed or put in flames and systematic looting shall be addressed with the relevant Croatian authorities." Can you please tell the Chamber who the relevant Croatian authorities were about whom -- or with whom you were going to address this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: General Cermak, here I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to admit 65 ter 4134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P1163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1163 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have 65 ter 4221. And, Mr. Al-Alfi, this is tab number 12 in your binder. And this is a report dated 8 September. And if we could move to page 3 in the English version. And this is where you indicated had you a meeting with General Cermak on 7 September at the beginning of the second full paragraph, and in the B/C/S, this appears on the second page at the fifth full paragraph. You state: "During the meeting we raised with General Cermak the question of continuing looting and burning of houses in the area. We further raised specific cases of recent murders which were brought to his attention and asked for the results of the investigation by the Croatian authorities. General Cermak did not deny the continuation of such activities, and said that strict orders have been issued to arrest those who commit such crimes." Now, further down, at the last sentence in this paragraph you state: "General Cermak agreed to give his instructions for more joint patrolling between UN CIVPOL and the Croatian police, particularly in the remote villages." Now, Mr. Al-Alfi, from your dealings with General Cermak, can you explain to the Chamber what your understanding was of General Cermak's authority to give instructions to civilian police?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: As I told you, after the fall of Knin, or what used to be Sector South, we had in writing, our headquarters had in writing from the Croatian government that General Cermak is the military governor of the area. So anything we have to report to him, that means he is the highest official to us. That's why we take any report of anything that he is in control or supervising anything or all components of the Croatian presence in that area, including the -- their civil police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you explain a little bit about how these joint patrols between UN CIVPOL and Croatian civilian police originated and what General Cermak's role was in that process?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: If you see, this report was 8 September, but this was that he agreed but -- and will give instructions. Whether this was implemented immediately, no. It was -- it has taken, in fact, in some very minor cases that it was joint patrolling. And others, we were -- this was not implemented at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to talk briefly about the Grubori incident in the Plavno valley, Mr. Al-Alfi. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could tender 65 ter 4221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1164 is admitted into evidence, in the absence of any objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 4174.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar. My apologies. If we could bring up 65 ter 6494. It's actually a much more legible version of 4174. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Al-Alfi, this appears at tab 19 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for reference, when you punch 6494 into e-court, you get two documents. One is the one Mr. Russo mentions, and the other one appears not to be related at all to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If that's a problem, we'll correct it, Your Honour, but I'm only interested in the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, you will see that this is a letter from General Cermak to you, indicating that it is a follow-up to a discussion you had with General Cermak on the 29th of August, 1995, in respect of the incident which happened in Grubori. Do you recall, Mr. Al-Alfi, the incident that happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: As I said, I reported that, and I said it in my statement that one of the reports I received from my civil affairs officers or political and humanitarian affairs officers that this incident happened. I took it to General Cermak, and General Cermak, to explain what happened. And if you see even in my statements, I said that one was killed, and because there was somebody killed at a later stage even after the operation which was reported, and then they gave even the name of that person, so that was a response, clarifying what action his army or his -- under his authority was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we look at third paragraph in this letter, General Cermak blames the incident on enemy raiders and terrorists, and he states: "Due to armed clashes and the use of bazookas, several barns and houses caught fire resulting in death of two unidentified women and two elderly men (Milos Grubor and Jovo Grubor) who succumbed to trajectory wounds." And in the last sentence of this letter, General Cermak states: "I personally visited the hamlet the following day and verified myself that events took the course as described above." Mr. Al-Alfi, did General Cermak ever explain to you how he verified that this version of events is what took place?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move for the admission of 65 ter 4174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are you referring to the better legible copy which is 6494, which is then should --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, I move for 6494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6494, and then only this one page. Mr. Registrar, this one page of 6494 would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1165 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, before finishing, I'd like to show you a letter that you wrote to General Cermak upon his departure from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 3444.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in your binder, Mr. Al-Alfi, this appears at tab 16. This is a letter dated 22 November 1995, and in the second sentence of the third paragraph, Mr. Al-Alfi, you state: "It was a great pleasure for me to work with you during your service as commander of the Knin military post. Your professionalism and sense of responsibility and concern about the solution of the problems this area is faced with will long be remembered." Do you recall sending this letter to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But I don't see anything wrong in it. Because I dealt with him, he was representing the local authorities. I was representing the United Nations, and we have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not an accusation. It is just a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Al-Alfi, I'm certainly not accusing of you anything. I just wanted to know if you could describe for the chamber how in your view General Cermak demonstrated a sense of responsibility for the issues that you had raised with him.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: In my opinion, a sense of responsibility at least when I asked to him, he would not reject. When I talk, he would listen to me. Whether he takes action, that is something else. To me, that is professionalism. Listen to the other side, see what you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, based on all of the meetings that you had with General Cermak and all of the times as some that we've seen that you have advised him about burning, looting, and other human rights violations, can you tell the Court from your perspective whether you believe that General Cermak did anything about the issues that you brought to his attention?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, I will not put it whether he did or not. Whether things have changed, I would say not many. But whether he did or not, that's something he will not report to me what he did. So it's not for me to judge whether he took personally any action or not. But in some case, as I said, there was nothing more to do damage to, so the destruction is done, and the situation has changed gradually from many houses in flames to no more houses to be looted or to be in flames. So all I would say, I don't know how it happened. Whether it was him or somebody else, that I don't know. But, to me, I saw that the situation has changed and -- at least the burning stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness. I will tender 3444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1166 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do have no further questions for the witness, Your Honour. However, I did want to tender the remaining exhibits which were submitted to the Defence and to the Chamber. I understand that there are outstanding objections to three of those documents. I can certainly send the list of those which remain to be submitted to the registrar, and then we can tender them en masse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your 12 December prosecution submission of associated exhibits motion to add one witness related document. Is that the one we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It is it, Your Honour. However I did submit an updated spreadsheet. Mr. Kuzmanovic mentioned to Chambers yesterday that included taking out one extra document and adding the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have that on my ... We know that objections were raised in relation to three of these documents. As far as the others are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. Just as a technical matter, Your Honour, at page 48, lines 15 to 17, you indicated that the Chamber would like to have a look at the three documents that are objected to. I don't know if Your Honours' intent was to see them in court, or if you wish to see them in Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily in court, I would say. Yes, if you could remind me of the numbers, the correct numbers, then I could find them on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do the 65 ter numbers, Your Honour. For those it would be 65 ter 4125. 65 ter 4133. And 65 ter 4252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, could I receive an indication from the Defence, first what the order will be of the examination, the cross-examination of Mr. Al-Alfi; and second, a time indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will be first. I anticipate a day with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will be second, Your Honour, and I anticipate no more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will go last, Your Honour, and I anticipate no more than an hour as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which would mean that we could not finish on the 17th, so mostly likely we'll finish on the 17th -- no, 18th. I'm mistaken. Mr. Al-Alfi, we have questions for you up to the 18th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm at your disposal, Your Honour, although I was informed that I will be able to travel tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that might turn out not -- of course, the parties will do their utmost best to keep you here as briefly as possible. But it's, of course, a fair opportunity should be given of cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, let's then not lose any time. You will first be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Al-Alfi, the first question I'm going to ask you about concerns your statement and interview. It's Exhibit P1160, and of that document I would like you to turn to page 64. And it's your tape-recorded interview, and you're being questioned by someone called Kellie Ward, and you answer those questions, and you will see at the line 23, Kellie Ward says: "We were discussing Cermak prior to turning the tape over. For the purpose of this interview, could you tell me what Cermak actually had control over and how far his authority stretched." Your Honour, answer was: "I don't know exactly how." Kellie Ward then announced: "Taped record of our conversation suspended. Mr. Al-Alfi, could you tell me the time please." You answer: "I'm sorry, it's 3.18." She then says: "Suspended for a short time." Let us move to the next page. Conversation resumes at 3.35. So the suspension was in the order of 15 minutes. And the interview resumes: "Thank you." And she says: "Prior to the suspension, we were discussing Mr. Cermak, and I asked you if you could please explain to me what you believed his area of responsibility to be." She didn't add the answer you had previously given on the other page, I don't know exactly how, but you then give a very long answer about him being a military commander or having responsibility of a military commander, and we can see there what the answer was. I'm interested to know what happened in that 15 minutes, Mr. Al-Alfi, and what was said to you, because there is no explanation on the record. The rest of your interview, when there is adjournments - your daughter making a cup of tea, you answering the door, some other reason, there is always an explanation. I would like you to tell us what happened in that 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: It's very clear if you notice -- I don't recall exactly what happened. But if you noticed on the page 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: The question on number 23, the question was: You tell me what Cermak -- whether -- what Cermak actually had control over. Control over. So it's not a question of control. It's not my judgement. But when the question later on was rephrased -- why it stopped, I don't recall. At this moment, I don't recall why this break was. But the question was rephrased to be: What you believed his area of responsibility to be. That I can answer, whether he was in actual control, that I cannot answer. That's why you can see why the question was also rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But what was said to you during that suspension of the taped interview that could not go on the record? What was said to you, because the questioner suspends the interview so that when I look at this years later, I can't see what was said. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall why it was stopped. At this moment, I don't recall why it was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there a discussion about what you should say?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there a discussion about the question?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, to my best recollection, there was no discussion about the question, because everything was on tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't, was it?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: No, that part -- if the tape was stopped there was no discussion about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because then you move from, I don't know exactly how, to a changed question and then an answer.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Well, to me, it -- maybe to clarify the question, she rephrased it, but to me, it's almost whether I knew whether he is in control, and that's something different from what I believe his responsibility is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go through now the reports that you have been able to produce that have been authored by you or sent by you, and the first document that we look at will be the first one in time, Exhibit P1161.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we're getting that on the screen, Your Honour, we haven't prepared a disclosure list of exhibits yet because originally this witness was going to be viva voce, and he has turn into a 92 ter today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your expectation was that cross-examination would start later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I will be using just today Prosecution documents that we have through them, and we will be preparing a list of any other documents in the light of Mr. Russo's questioning today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to go through these reports, and so it's going to take a little time, but I think it is it important, Mr. Al-Alfi. This is the first document, and we're going to look at the meetings in your reports that have taken place with General Cermak to see what the record is as written by you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: I do. But can you identify which report you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking at the one of 8th of August. It's at 1640 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe that's tab 2 in the witness's binder. I will e-mail -- Your Honours, just to make this a little easier, I'll e-mail to the Defence a spreadsheet that shows the tab numbers for each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you got the document?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It will always come up on the screen in front of you as well, if you need any guidance. This is your first report, and we see that in paragraph 1: "We were informed by General Cermak ... military governor in the area ... about the Croatian army starting to pull out of the main cities." If we look at your report of what was said by General Cermak, there is no sentence here indicating burning, looting, or crimes. It concerns the matters that we see in the document, but there is no mention of burnings, lootings, and crimes in your meeting with General Cermak. Accordingly, that was not a matter raised or discussed by you at that meeting with him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: This was an introductory meeting, as you notice the date is 8. As I said, this was the first time we were out of our compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but my proposition is right, and you record what your meeting was about with General Cermak, that it concerned military and civilian police, civilian authorities expecting to arrive in Knin, other matters, freedom of movement. But it does not raise the issue of crimes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: At that time, as I said, it was a introductory meeting, so we were knowing what are the responsibilities of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will look at the next document. This is 65 ter 4755. It's a bar table document, and it's a record with a time of 2055.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it refers, as you can see, to your meeting that morning, to General Cermak, and representatives of the displaced persons in the UNCRO compound. And we can see the discussion in that meeting of what was being offered to the displaced persons, rights. We can see at paragraph 4, a discussion concerning dead bodies being found, 90 per cent of them military, and the focal point in this regard being Dr. Brkic, chief of the sanitary unit, and we can see that there was a discussion about soldiers who didn't commit war crimes, displaced persons. Again, nothing mentioned there about looting and burning or crimes in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could the screen be changed to the next paragraph, please. Thank you very much. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've looked at this, Mr. Al-Alfi. Nothing there in this report about lootings, burnings, or killings being raised by you to General Cermak at this meeting. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: If you notice --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: -- this is the same -- the report is on the same day as the previous report. It was only less than -- or around four hours between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: From the timing, okay? And according to the first meeting we had, General Cermak said that he wanted to meet these people, to talk to them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN AL-ALFI
utterances.text: -- who were in our compound. We allowed him. The occasion was talking specifically to those who were displaced inside our compound. It's not a general situation. It is a report on this meeting in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't disagree, and thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D1208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the document is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since apparently you want to move to another subject or at least another document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. It would be continuing through these documents, Your Honour, and it would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I find on the bar table list, 65 ter number -- which apparently is a 6152, which is the one only tentatively given a 65 ter number. I heard of no objections against admission of that document. May I take that to include no objections against adding it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would be using it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then as far as 4125 is concerned, could we receive information as what is the paragraph or is it the whole of the document which would meet the objections, 4125 being the 23rd of August document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would have an objection to paragraphs 1 through 6, and in theory -- yes, I guess paragraph 7 mentions the Gracac cemetery, so might be of some relevance. But paragraphs one through six deal with matters that are not in the Split Military District or the Knin municipality. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next one being 4133. What paragraphs would it be? And that's the 24th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Paragraphs 1 through 5 are outside of the Split Military District or the Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And six would then be within again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the last one is 4252, and that would be -- that's the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as I can tell, this entire document concerns matters that are outside of the Split Military District and the Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection covers the whole of the document. Thank you, Mr. Misetic. We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Al-Alfi. We resume tomorrow, the 17th of December, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
